Making any plans for the future
I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking

Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When I remember the event I feel intense shame

vignette: Eleanor Vance spent three decades reading radiographic films in quiet rooms, but the siege at a field hospital when she was thirty-six shattered that stillness. Trapped for weeks as artillery turned corridors into charnel houses, she survived the night the generators failed. That event never arrived as a coherent story; it surfaced only as a nonverbal cascade of heat, the copper tang of blood, and the visceral terror of watching life bleed out while she adjusted a broken dial. When these fragments surfaced, a heavy shame settled over her. The harder she tried to deliberately recall the night, the more violently the nonverbal fragments intruded, and this difficulty in accessing the memory quickly translated into a sweeping threat perception. She began to read the world as the war zone had been: every unfamiliar hospital wing felt like unassessed territory, and the quiet approach of a nurse in her radiology reading room triggered the same hypervigilant alarm as strangers closing in during the siege. Because facing the event felt like reliving helplessness, the shame of recall soon dictated her daily life. She developed a rigid habit of avoiding anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, preferring a flat existence. This emotional numbness made making any plans for the future impossible, as looking ahead felt like stepping into unknown ground. To quiet the panic, she retreated into screen escape, spending long hours on her phone or games to avoid thinking. Yet this avoidance of feelings and digital distraction did not seal the trauma away. Instead, the emotional void they created became a pressure cooker, and her maladaptive strategies directly fed back into her memory processing. When she finally set the phone down, the suppressed fragments would surge forward with renewed intensity, proving that the very tactics she used to numb the shame only ensured the memory would continue to demand attention. As the years passed, her refusal to engage reshaped her professional routine. Her habit of avoiding all feelings meant she no longer trusted her emotional compass, which amplified her threat system. She began to scan for danger in every clinical environment, her eyes darting to exits and monitors as if expecting collapse. The avoidance of future plans left her chronically anchored in the present, stripping away continuity. Without long-term goals, her maladaptive strategies funneled all her remaining cognitive energy into threat monitoring. When colleagues approached her reading room, the absence of a forward-looking safety net meant her brain defaulted to immediate alarm. Threat from strangers became her default posture, and scanning for danger turned her workspace into a perimeter she had to constantly secure. The cycle tightened through her seventies. Eleanor’s constant scanning and the acute threat she felt from approaching strangers created perpetual physiological arousal that directly destabilized her memory boundaries. The more she braced for danger, the more readily her brain pulled forth the fragmented, nonverbal traces of the siege. Her occupational life had frayed; she could no longer read films without her hands trembling, and the hospital offered medical retirement. What finally brought her to my office was the exhaustion of maintaining a fortress around a self that no longer felt like her own. She hoped to find a way to step out of the screening room of her mind, though her deepest fear remained that opening the door would let the war back in.
